narrative:
The model predicted a 73.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Being in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) is far below the average of roughly 6 among students who were accepted. Your first-year ranking was the second most important factor and similarly pulled the outcome toward failure; again you placed in the bottom decile while accepted students averaged around 6.

Your undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction. At 3.80 it is noticeably higher than the 3.23 average of accepted students, which helped reduce the predicted risk of failure. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the impact of your low class rankings.

Your LSAT score of 39, upper-middle family income, and plan to attend full-time were all close to or better than typical accepted students, but they carried less weight in the final decision.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic standing in law school so that your class rank improves significantly by the end of the third year. Stronger performance there would directly address the factor that most hurt your prediction. Consider reapplying once you have demonstrated that improvement.
